Monday-Wednesday morning: An unsettled weather pattern will 
remain over the Northwest delivering periods of rain and 
generally warmer than normal temperatures. The cold front that 
swept through Sunday morning has weakened and is draped across 
northern Oregon. This boundary coupled with a heavy influx of 
Pacific moisture is slowly lifting back northward today as 
midlevel flow veers from the west to southwest ahead the next 
trough crossing 140W. Forcing will be weak through today but 
appreciable moisture will result in mostly cloudy skies with 
spit and spats of light rain through the day. Rain will pick-up 
region-wide by the late afternoon/evening and continue into the 
overnight hours as a stronger, occluding front sweeps inland. A 
majority of the region will receive between a tenth and two 
tenths of an inch. Lower amounts (less than a tenth) are
expected across the Camas Prairie and L-C Valley. Locally higher
amounts > 0.25 inches for the Selkirks of North Idaho and
Northeastern WA, and upwards of 0.40-1.00 inches for the 
Cascade Crest and upper river valleys of the East Slopes.

A short lived break arrives in the rain early Tuesday morning 
then a stronger warm front with subtropical moisture draped 
across it will lift through the region during the day and north 
of the International border by Tuesday night. Overall, rains 
will mainly be beneficial for the Inland NW with mild 
temperatures suggesting little to no concerns for winter travel 
conditions. The main area for light snow (1-3 inches) will be
Washington Pass. Otherwise, the main impacts to travel will 
come in the form of fog, possibly dense at times each night and 
morning.


A second concern, and this comes with low confidence, will be the 
compounding effects of several days of on and off rain over the
Cascade burn scars and whether showers Monday evening or the 
last bout of stratiform on Tuesday will be enough to trigger a 
debris flow. The intensity of the stratiform rain over the last 
few days is not very conducive to debris flows but soils are 
becoming saturated with rain falling every 24 hours over the 
last 3 days. Showers Monday evening will be capable of slightly 
heavier rates with HRRR indicating ranges from 0.01 to 0.20" and
locally near 0.30 closer to the crest around Stehekin. We will 
need to closely monitor this activity Monday evening. Following 
the short break, focus will shift toward the next warm front and
period of rain on Tuesday. Around the Little Giant, Sisi, and 
Pioneer burn scars, 6 hour rainfall amounts vary from 0.20 to 
0.60 from the 10th to 90th percentile leading to a mean around 
0.30". 

Wednesday-Thursday: A sharper and colder trough carves into the E Pac 
around midweek allowing high pressure to amplify over the 
Inland NW. This will bring a break from the wet weather with the
next axis of moisture aimed into southwestern British Columbia.
The main impacts for the area will be breezy south to southeast
winds and mild temperatures. NBM is indicating a few areas 
around Lewiston approaching record warmth with highs in the mid 
60s. Overnight lows will also be mild. This flow pattern in the 
boundary is favorable for persistent low clouds across the 
mountain valleys of northern WA and Cascades and potential for 
dense fog to develop where surface winds are light. Many areas 
outside of the Palouse and L-C Valley will be susceptible.

Friday-Monday: There is good agreement amongst the ensemble 
suites for the colder offshore trough to track inland as the 
ridge axis shift into the Northern Plains. This has potential 
for a more impactful late fall storm system with rain switching 
back to snow for the mountains and mountain passes, gusty winds,
and return to more seasonal, and colder temperatures. Roughly 
80% of the ensembles support this pattern change. The precise 
details still come with moderate uncertainty, particularly what 
day the leading cold front arrives Friday or Saturday? Current 
outlook suggest passes will remain snow free for travel on 
Friday, possibly Saturday as well but confidence decreases 
rapidly by Saturday night into Sunday. /sb
